title: The sister who saw first
hookLine: his older sister, Bebe Nanaki, is remembered as the first to recognize who her brother was

lines: A BOY WHO WORRIES THE VILLAGE.
cards: A dreamy boy is worrying the grown-ups of his village. In the stories the janamsakhis tell, he gives things away. He sits silent for hours.
He asks the village priest and teacher questions they can't answer. His father, Mehta Kalu, loves him and worries constantly: how will this boy ever earn a living?
But one person watches him with a different kind of attention, and believes in him before there is much evidence. His big sister.

teach.b: Her name was Nanaki. Sikhs call her Bebe Nanaki: bebe is an affectionate word for an older sister or a respected woman. Tradition says she was about five years older than Nanak.
To everyone else, her brother was a puzzle. Nanaki saw it differently.
Sikh tradition remembers her as the first to recognize that he wasn't lost. He was found, in a way the others couldn't see yet.
Some Sikhs even call her the first Sikh, the first follower of the Guru, though she was his sister before she was anything else. And she didn't stop at believing.
Nanaki married a man named Jai Ram and moved to the town of Sultanpur. When her brother was a young man, drifting and at odds with his father, she brought him there.
Jai Ram helped find him work, and Nanak lived near her for years.
The turning point of his life, a few days from now, happened in Sultanpur, because she made room for him. The sources say little about her own inner life, and that's worth saying.
What they remember is the shape of her love: she saw him first, and she made space for what she saw.

how: Sikhs honor Bebe Nanaki as Guru Nanak's devoted older sister, often called the first to recognize him; a gurdwara in her memory stands in Sultanpur Lodhi.

games.why: Nanaki brought him to Sultanpur, and Jai Ram helped find him work. some of the biggest moments of his life happened there.

practice: Let a face come to mind: someone who believed in you early, before there was much to go on. Hear their voice, remember one thing they said, and let the gratitude come without rushing.
Then say the one sentence you'd tell them now, quietly or on paper.
